text: SERIALIZABLE is the strictest of the four ANSI isolation levels. Set it the same way as the others, and it guarantees that running the same query twice in one transaction returns not just the same values, but the exact same set of rows -- no phantoms either.
It's the only standard level that prevents all three classic anomalies at once: dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads.

How? REPEATABLE READ couldn't stop a phantom because it only locks rows it has already read -- there's nothing to lock for a row that doesn't exist yet. SERIALIZABLE uses a fundamentally different lock: a range lock, which locks the entire gap a predicate describes, not just the rows that happen to match right now. An insert of a new row falling inside that locked range gets blocked until the transaction finishes.

That protection isn't free. Range locks can block entirely new inserts, not just updates to rows that already exist -- which makes SERIALIZABLE the most blocking of any standard isolation level. This is the strictest point on the dial we introduced back in the first lesson of this cluster.

So reach for SERIALIZABLE deliberately, not by default -- when a specific piece of business logic genuinely cannot tolerate a phantom row appearing or disappearing mid-calculation. For most everyday code, REPEATABLE READ or even plain READ COMMITTED is enough, and costs far less concurrency.
That wraps up the four ANSI standard levels. Next lesson, we leave locking behind entirely and look at SQL Server's own approach: SNAPSHOT isolation, built on row versioning instead. See you there.
